Standard errors for means and SDs imputed from five-number summaries

Source: vignettes/fivenumMeta.Rmd
fivenumMeta.Rmd

The problem, and what this package does

Many studies in a meta-analysis report a median with the quartiles, or with the minimum and the maximum, instead of the sample mean and sample standard deviation (SD). The established estimators (Wan, Luo and Shi, and the best linear unbiased estimators from the reported values) impute population mean and standard deviation parameters from such a summary. In the pooling stage of a meta-analysis, such imputed mean and SD estimators are often treated as the sample mean and sample SD, with the naive standard errors of the sample mean and sample SD. However, the imputed estimators are generally less precise than the sample estimators. Thus their variations/uncertainties should be accounted for.

This package computes, under normality, how much less precise. The standard deviation of the imputed mean is Cμ(n)σC_\mu(n)\,\sigma and that of the imputed SD is Cσ(n)σC_\sigma(n)\,\sigma, with factors that depend on the sample size, on which values were reported, on the estimator and on the definition of the sample quantiles, and not on the data. The package computes the factors exactly from the means and covariances of the normal order statistics. It returns the plug-in standard errors Cμ(n)σ̂C_\mu(n)\,\hat\sigma and Cσ(n)σ̂C_\sigma(n)\,\hat\sigma that belong in the weights of a meta-analysis.

At a sample size of 25, the standard deviation of the imputed mean exceeds σ/n\sigma/\sqrt n by 8% when the three quartiles are reported, by 13% when the minimum, median and maximum are reported, and by 3% when all five values are. The standard deviation of the imputed SD exceeds that of a sample SD by 65%, 26% and 10% in the same three cases. With only the minimum, median and maximum reported, the excess grows with the sample size, to 24% and 243% at a sample size of 1001.

The evidence on a public data set

The example data set comes from the meta-analysis of Katzenschlager et al. (2021) of the age of COVID-19 patients who died against those who survived, shipped with the metamedian package as dat.age: 51 studies, two groups each, of which 29 report the quartiles and 22 a mean and SD. The call below imputes the mean and SD of each group where they are missing, keeps the sample ones where they are not, and appends the difference of means (nonsurvivors minus survivors) with its standard error under the naive rule and under the exact factors. The quartiles are taken under R’s default definition (type 7), the package’s default. A study that states another definition is given its type.

d <- se_imputed_diff(
  data     = metamedian::dat.age,   # one row per study
  suffixes = c(".g1", ".g2"),       # the two groups' suffixes, group 1 first
  version  = "blue"                 # the BLUE (default) or "wan_luo_shi"
)
str(d)   # the input columns, each group's output columns, the difference
#> 'data.frame':    51 obs. of  32 variables:

The result keeps every input column and appends, for each group with its suffix, the scenario read off the row, the imputed or sample mean and SD, and the three standard errors, then the difference yi with its standard errors sei_naive and sei. The section “Where to look afterwards” defines each column. pool_imputed() pools the studies under the naive and the exact standard errors side by side, with the common-effect model by default:

fit <- pool_imputed(d)
fit
#> Pooled difference of means (group 1 minus group 2), common-effect model (EE), 51 studies
#>          estimate     se ci.lb ci.ub pval     Q    I2
#> naive SE    11.89 0.2715 11.35 12.42    0 443.7 88.73
#> exact SE    11.92 0.2853 11.36 12.48    0 401.1 87.53
#> 95% confidence intervals and p-values from the normal distribution. Q has 50 degrees of freedom, and I2 is in percent.
#> The weights in percent are $weights. Every field with str() or unclass().

The estimates, standard errors and interval limits are in years and I2I^2 is in percent. For the random-effects model, metafor takes the same columns (here with REML):

re_naive <- metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei_naive, data = d)   # random effects, REML
re_exact <- metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d)
row <- function(fit) {
  c(estimate = as.numeric(fit$b), se = fit$se, ci.lb = fit$ci.lb,
    ci.ub = fit$ci.ub, tau2 = fit$tau2, I2 = fit$I2)
}
round(rbind(`naive SE` = row(re_naive), `exact SE` = row(re_exact)), 3)
#>          estimate    se  ci.lb  ci.ub   tau2     I2
#> naive SE   13.342 0.863 11.650 15.034 30.663 88.830
#> exact SE   13.343 0.862 11.653 15.033 30.087 87.626

τ2\tau^2 is in years squared.

Three things can be read off the output. First, for every study that reports quartiles, the exact standard error of its imputed mean is 5.5% to 7.7% larger than the naive one, so such a study carries 2% to 5% less weight. Under the common-effect model, the share of the weight on the quartile studies falls from 69.9% to 66.7%, and the pooled standard error rises by 5.1%. Second, under the random-effects model the pooled difference moves by 0.1% of its standard error, and the standard error itself by 0.1%, because the between-study variance dominates the total there (I2I^2 of 89%). Third, τ2\tau^2 is smaller under the exact standard errors, 30.1 against 30.7, because larger within-study variances leave less of the spread of the estimates to be read as heterogeneity.

The calls to use: se_imputed_diff() for two groups per row, se_imputed_df() for one, and pool_imputed() to pool, with version = "blue" (the default). version = "wan_luo_shi" gives the estimators of Wan, Luo and Shi instead, for comparability with an earlier analysis. For a meta-analysis of SDs, se_imputed_diff(..., measure = "lnVR") gives the log variability ratio of the two groups with its two standard errors, as the second vignette shows.

Setup: the columns and the scenarios

se_imputed_df() takes one row per study and reads these columns, each named by an argument with the default shown, with a suffix appended for data sets that carry two groups side by side:

Argument Default column Holds
n n the sample size
min, max min, max the minimum and the maximum
q1, med, q3 q1, med, q3 the first quartile, the median, the third quartile
mean, sd mean, sd the sample mean and SD, where a study gives them

A column that the data set does not have, or an argument set to NULL, counts as absent for every row, and a missing value counts as absent for that row. The scenario of a row is read off the values present: all five give S3S_3; the three quartiles give S2S_2; the minimum, median and maximum give S1S_1; a sample mean and SD with no summary give “sample”, whose standard error is sd / sqrt(n); and a mean with the minimum and the maximum and no SD gives “mean_range”, where the mean is kept and the SD is imputed from the range. A row with both a summary and a sample mean and SD follows prefer, which is "sample" by default because the sample statistics are the direct measurement. A row with none of these, with a missing sample size, with values out of order, or whose standard errors would be zero (a sample SD of zero, a summary whose values are all equal) gets NA in every output column and is named in one warning with its reason. The function does not stop, so the whole table comes back. Output columns left by an earlier call are replaced.

The factors are computed exactly at every sample size. At n=4Q+1n = 4Q + 1 the reported quartiles are single order statistics. At any other sample size each reported quantile is a fixed combination of two neighboring order statistics, by R’s default definition (type 7 of quantile()) unless the argument type names another, and the factors there depend on that definition. The closed-form shortcut formulas of Appendix A are within half a percent of the exact factors at every sample size n=4Q+1n = 4Q + 1 from 5 to 1001.

Where to look afterwards

Each group’s output columns carry its suffix.

Column What it holds
scenario "S1", "S2", "S3", "sample" or "mean_range", as read off the row
mu_hat, sigma_hat the imputed mean and SD, or the sample ones
se_naive σ̂/n\hat\sigma/\sqrt n, the standard error that treats the imputed mean as a sample mean
se_mu Cμ(n)σ̂C_\mu(n)\,\hat\sigma, the exact plug-in standard error of the imputed mean (for a sample mean, sd / sqrt(n))
se_sigma Cσ(n)σ̂C_\sigma(n)\,\hat\sigma, the exact plug-in standard error of the imputed SD (for a sample SD, the standard deviation of a sample SD under normality with the SD plugged in)
version_used "blue", "wan_luo_shi" or "sample"
exact TRUE for a row with an imputed value, whose factors are computed exactly at its sample size, NA for a sample row

se_imputed_diff() adds yi, the effect of the study, with sei_naive and sei, its standard errors from the naive and from the exact standard errors, the two groups’ variances added. By default the effect is the difference of the two means (group 1 minus group 2), and measure = "lnVR" makes it the log variability ratio, the log of the SD of group 1 over the SD of group 2. pool_imputed() pools these columns under both standard errors, and metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei) takes them as they are.

The vignette two-meta-analyses reproduces the two meta-analyses of Wu, Shi and Tong (2026): a meta-analysis of means in which studies report the median and the range, on the data set vitd that ships with the package, and a meta-analysis of SDs in which studies report the quartiles, on this data set.

Appendix A. The factors by scenario

inflation_factors() returns the ratio of the standard deviation of the imputed mean to that of the sample mean, κμ(n)=Cμ(n)n\kappa_\mu(n) = C_\mu(n)\sqrt n, and the ratio of the standard deviation of the imputed SD to that of the sample SD, κσ(n)\kappa_\sigma(n), for the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE, the default) or the estimators of Wan, Luo and Shi (version = "wan_luo_shi").

grid <- c(5, 25, 101, 1001)
tab <- sapply(c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
              function(sc) sapply(grid, function(n) inflation_factors(n, sc)))
rownames(tab) <- paste0(rep(c("kappa_mu", "kappa_sigma"), length(grid)),
                        ", n = ", rep(grid, each = 2))
round(tab, 3)
#>                          S1    S2    S3
#> kappa_mu, n = 5       1.026 1.063 1.000
#> kappa_sigma, n = 5    1.089 1.683 1.070
#> kappa_mu, n = 25      1.131 1.075 1.034
#> kappa_sigma, n = 25   1.255 1.652 1.105
#> kappa_mu, n = 101     1.200 1.077 1.057
#> kappa_sigma, n = 101  1.705 1.650 1.253
#> kappa_mu, n = 1001    1.244 1.078 1.074
#> kappa_sigma, n = 1001 3.427 1.650 1.507

Under S2S_2 both factors are nearly constant in the sample size. Under S1S_1 both grow with it: κμ(n)\kappa_\mu(n) toward its limit π/2\sqrt{\pi/2}, about 25% above one, and κσ(n)\kappa_\sigma(n) without bound, because Cσ(n)C_\sigma(n) decays only like 1/log⁡n1/\log n there while the standard deviation of a sample SD decays like 1/n1/\sqrt n. Under S3S_3 the extremes help at small sample sizes and the factors move toward those of S2S_2 as the sample grows. The closed-form shortcut formulas c_mu_shortcut() and c_sigma_shortcut() give the factors Cμ(n)C_\mu(n) and Cσ(n)C_\sigma(n) without the integration, for a reader without this package and for comparison:

c(exact = c_mu(25, "S2"), shortcut = c_mu_shortcut(25, "S2"))
#>     exact  shortcut 
#> 0.2150631 0.2149903
c(exact = c_sigma(25, "S2"), shortcut = c_sigma_shortcut(25, "S2"))
#>     exact  shortcut 
#> 0.2372150 0.2374137

Appendix B. One study at a time

se_imputed() takes one study’s reported values and sample size.

se_imputed(c(q1 = 10, med = 12, q3 = 15), n = 25, scenario = "S2")
#> Imputed mean and SD under S2, n = 25, the BLUE, quantile type 7
#>    mu_hat sigma_hat  se_naive     se_mu  se_sigma 
#>   12.3575    3.9252    0.7850    0.8442    0.9311 
#> Factors: C_mu(n) = 0.2151, C_sigma(n) = 0.2372. The weights are $w_mean and $w_sd; every field with str() or unclass().

The imputed mean is the median pulled a little toward the mid-quartile range, the imputed SD is a multiple of the interquartile range, and the exact standard error of the mean exceeds the naive one by the factor of the table above at n=25n = 25 under S2S_2.
